nh_triple_corners_center.blurb: The middle stretch of the Triple Corners cliff band at Rumney holds sixteen routes, split between trad and bolted lines with a single top-rope. Grades run from easy 5.3 up through the low 5.12s, and the heart of the spread sits between 5.8 and 5.11. A fourth-class gully cuts up through the centre of the wall and is best avoided when it is wet; above it sit about six good lines that photograph well. The harder bolted routes cluster toward the left end of the wider Triple Corners area, while moderate 5.8 to 5.10 climbing is easier to find toward the right.

nh_quartz_block.blurb: A single bouldering block at Rumney, grouped with the Entrance Boulders inside the larger Black Jack Boulders zone. It packs sixteen problems into one spot, so a session here is about working a handful of lines rather than hiking between boulders. Most of the problems fall between V0 and V3, which suits climbers warming up or building up to harder grades, and a few go well past that, with the hardest reaching V8. A couple of the best-regarded lines in the V3 to V5 range are marked as having a serious landing, so spot carefully.

nh_saco_crag.blurb: A small, wooded granite crag in the North Conway valley, tucked in the trees just above West Side Road. Nearly all of its sixteen routes are trad, with one bolted line, and they run from about 5.6 to the low 5.12s, though most sit between 5.8 and 5.10. Walking up to the base takes only a couple of minutes on a steep, dirty path. The top is easy to reach by scrambling around the side and has plenty of trees, which makes the cliff a handy spot for setting up top-ropes on moderate lines. Reports describe it as shady and cool on hot days.
nh_saco_crag.approach: A short, steep, rough trail leads up from the road to the base of the cliff.

nh_pulse_wall.blurb: A small schist wall at Rumney made up of short, broken sections that climb with a bouldery feel. Its fifteen routes mix nine sport lines with six trad lines, and the range is wide: a few easy climbs near 5.4 to 5.5, a handful in the 5.7 to 5.10 range, and a cluster of hard sport routes in the 5.11 and 5.12 grades. Styles go from cracks to steep, sustained face climbing. The wall sits off the main trails and sees few visitors, so it tends to be quiet. The steep centrepiece line is the area's best-known route.

nh_02_gulley_no_1_buttress.blurb: A steeper, one-pitch buttress on Mt. Willard in Crawford Notch, quite different in feel from the long slab routes on the main face. The fifteen climbs are mostly traditional lines, with a single bolted route, and almost all fall between 5.5 and 5.8, plus one 5.10 line. Protection is decent on many routes, though a few carry run-out ratings, and those can be top-roped with extra rope and long slings. It is a quiet alternative for moderate leaders in a mountain setting. Loose rock has been reported falling near the base, so keep an eye overhead.
nh_02_gulley_no_1_buttress.parking_note: Leave the car at a gravel pullout on the cliff side of Route 302 in Crawford Notch; a cairned trail from there heads toward Hattie's Garden in roughly ten minutes.

_expect.name: Kinsman Notch Ice (aka Luck O' The Irish crag)

nh_kinsman_notch_ice_aka_luck_o_the_iris.blurb: A winter ice and mixed crag in Kinsman Notch, above Route 112 near North Woodstock. Fifteen climbs are packed fairly close together: nine ice routes, mostly WI3 to WI4 with one at WI5, and six mixed lines from M5 up to M9. Thick woods keep sun off the ice and shelter the crag from wind. A steep path climbs from the road to the base, where crampons help when it is icy. The crag splits into a right-hand section near the top of the trail and a second section farther left. Many routes are easy to top-rope from trees, and weekends can get busy.
nh_kinsman_notch_ice_aka_luck_o_the_iris.parking_note: Pull off beside Route 112 in the notch; a steep climbers' path leads up to the crag from there.
